name: Abhijith U
intro: I turn complex systems into clear, considered experiences.
bio: I'm a UI/UX designer with a background in electrical and robotics engineering. I design mobile apps and websites, and I can build them in code.
about: Before design, I studied Electrical and Electronics Engineering, then completed an M.Tech in Robotics and Automation at the College of Engineering Trivandrum. For my master's thesis, I built an autonomous landmine detector using Raspberry Pi, Arduino, ROS and lidar.

Robotics taught me to think in systems: how the parts connect, where things break, and what happens next. I now bring that way of thinking to information architecture, interaction design and interface details.

I moved into UI/UX through Intellipaat's design certification and an internship at Zoople Technologies. Freelance mobile interface work gave me experience with user flows, wireframes and interactive prototypes. I also write HTML, CSS and Python.

projects.name: RepUp
projects.summary: A focused fitness experience that brings the next workout and meaningful progress into view.
projects.overview: RepUp brings guided workouts, personal plans and progress insights into one focused mobile experience. I worked from research and information architecture through a visual system and 23 high-fidelity screens.
projects.problemTitle: Starting a workout shouldn't feel like work.
projects.problem: Beginners felt overwhelmed by choices and unclear guidance. More experienced users wanted meaningful progress data without being treated like beginners. Both needed a clearer route from opening the app to getting started.
projects.researchNote: Project research: Google Forms survey (127 respondents) and eight interviews of 20–30 minutes. These are research findings, not measured product outcomes.
projects.quote: Too many features crammed into one screen. I just want to start my workout without digging through menus and settings.

process.title: Listen & define
process.text: A survey, eight interviews and a review of Nike Training Club, Peloton and MyFitnessPal surfaced two needs: guidance for beginners and useful data for experienced users.

process.title: Map the daily loop
process.text: I organized the experience into six sections and three core journeys: onboarding, the daily workout loop, and upgrading to Pro.

process.title: Build & refine
process.text: Low-fidelity wireframes established hierarchy before the high-fidelity system. Peer and target-user feedback informed layout and interaction refinements.

decisions.title: Put the next workout first
decisions.text: Today's workout has its own start action on Home. The design target was a route of three taps or fewer, responding to the 55% who asked for quick-start workouts.

decisions.title: Make progress a reason to return
decisions.text: The weekly chart appears on Home, while Insights and Progress reveal longer-term trends. This responds to the 68% who asked for visual tracking.

decisions.title: Ask only what shapes the plan
decisions.text: Weight, height and fitness level form a short onboarding sequence. The goal was a fast, relevant start; the under-one-minute target still needs timed validation.

projects.next: Design the active workout timer, completion flow and recovery states. Then test the time to start a workout and whether AI coaching adds enough value to earn its place.

editorial.title: Make the next step obvious.
editorial.text: For RepUp, focus means giving the daily workout a clear starting point, then letting progress provide a reason to return.
editorial.cover:
A little less friction.
A little more momentum.

projects.name: Meridian
projects.summary: A boutique travel concept with an editorial pace and a clear path from inspiration to inquiry.
projects.overview: Meridian is a fictional travel company built around regional specialists and bespoke itineraries. I designed the desktop homepage, Journal index, article page and a mobile homepage.
projects.problemTitle: Sell a sense of possibility, then make the next step obvious.
projects.problem: A catalogue of packages would work against Meridian's personal service. The challenge was to communicate place and expertise while keeping one action clear: starting a trip inquiry.

process.title: Define the visual world
process.text: Spruce, stone and brass colors pair with Instrument Serif and Hanken Grotesk. Coordinates and route markings make the travel identity specific.

process.title: Build a reusable system
process.text: I assembled the homepage with auto layout and reusable components, then extended the system into the Journal index and article page.

process.title: Refine with feedback
process.text: Mentor feedback led to a wider inquiry bar, a clearer way to view all journeys and a route motif in the hero. The homepage was then adapted to 440 px mobile.

decisions.title: Give the inquiry room to work
decisions.text: The inquiry bar grew from 720 px to the full 1200 px content width. Adding Trip style captures how someone wants to travel alongside where, when and with whom.

decisions.title: Make the route the signature
decisions.text: A dashed route with waypoints replaced less effective hero treatments. A mask and Smart Animate create its reveal in the Figma prototype.

decisions.title: Carry one idea across the system
decisions.text: Coordinates connect the latitude strip, destination photography and footer. The same editorial hierarchy carries through the Journal and its stories.

projects.next: Complete the mobile Journal pages and design the trip-inquiry flow. Test whether travellers naturally begin with the inquiry bar or explore signature routes first.

editorial.title: The journey starts with trust.
editorial.text: Meridian balances the feeling of a place with the practical next step: an inquiry shaped around the traveller.
editorial.cover:
A sense of place,
before you arrive.

projects.name: Zomato IA redesign
projects.summary: Reorganizing a crowded food experience around what people came to do.
projects.status: Unsolicited concept · not affiliated with Zomato
projects.overview: This project rethinks navigation and the core ordering journey. Its outputs are an information architecture and user flow, rather than high-fidelity app screens.
projects.problemTitle: Too many destinations. Too little direction.
projects.problem: In the version I audited, food delivery, dining, grocery and events competed for attention. Cuisine shortcuts, promotional banners and restaurant cards added more choices before a person could act on their intent.

process.title: Audit the structure
process.text: I mapped the existing verticals and identified competing navigation, content overload, unclear promotional hierarchy and redirects to separate services.

process.title: Group by intent
process.text: Card sorting and tree-testing methods informed the proposed structure. The case-study materials do not record a participant count or quantitative validation results.

process.title: Reveal information in context
process.text: Progressive disclosure shapes Home and the ordering journey: show the choices relevant to the task, then introduce detail when it is needed.

decisions.title: Keep four stable destinations
decisions.text: Home, Search, Orders and Account become fixed tabs. Blinkit and District remain reachable through deep links outside the core navigation.

decisions.title: Ask for intent before content
decisions.text: An Order in / Dine out toggle makes Home relevant to the immediate task. Six cuisine shortcuts and See all reduce the initial choice set.

decisions.title: Bring browsing and search together
decisions.text: People who know what they want search; others browse. Both routes converge on one restaurant page, followed by a consistent cart and checkout.

projects.next: Test findability with real users, compare the four-tab model against the audited structure, and test the Order in / Dine out split. Validate the number of cuisine shortcuts rather than treating six as settled.

editorial.title: Intent before inventory.
editorial.text: The Zomato proposal begins with what someone wants to do. The navigation and content then follow that choice.

projects.name: Verge
projects.tagline: A little space to think clearly.
projects.summary: Four thoughtful steps for working through a difficult personal decision.
projects.overview: Verge helps someone name a decision, rank what matters, reflect on their feelings and assess readiness. The concept explores a career decision about relocating for a new role.
projects.problemTitle: Not every reason belongs on the same side of a list.
projects.problem: A pros-and-cons list treats every reason as equal. Difficult decisions need room for personal priorities, uncertainty and the possibility that someone is not ready yet.

process.title: Name the decision
process.text: A simple first step asks what someone is weighing, with a category and optional context.

process.title: Find the priorities
process.text: Choose up to three priorities, identify worries and put the priorities in order.

process.title: Reflect, then review
process.text: Separate excitement from hesitation before reviewing the suggested direction and setting a personal readiness score.

decisions.title: Name it before solving it
decisions.text: The first screen reassures the user: No need to solve it yet. Optional context lowers the pressure to write a perfect answer.

decisions.title: Make the trade-off visible
decisions.text: Choosing three priorities from six, then ranking them, lets the review connect back to what this person values most.

decisions.title: Leave room for Not yet
decisions.text: The review proposes a direction but includes This feels right and Not yet, plus a readiness slider. Testing must establish whether its interpretation feels helpful or too prescriptive.

projects.next: Design the Not yet path and the follow-up after saving a decision. Test with people facing a real choice, especially whether the generated reflection overstates what their words imply.

editorial.title: Leave room for uncertainty.
editorial.text: Verge makes space for personal priorities and hesitation. A useful reflection should help someone think, without deciding for them.
editorial.cover:
A little space
to think clearly.

fieldNotes.title: The interface is only part of the system.
fieldNotes.text: Engineering taught me to look at connections. In design, I start with the journey: what brings someone here, what they need now, and where the experience takes them next.

fieldNotes.title: A detail should carry an idea.
fieldNotes.text: A route becomes a signature in Meridian. A progress chart gives RepUp a daily rhythm. I look for visual choices that make an experience more useful and more recognisable.
